[10 points] Suppose $h_{t} = h^{old}$ is constant over time. Characterize the steady-state level of technology, $A^{*}$, in terms of the model parameters {$\eta ,h^{old}$, A$^{world}, \gamma$ }. How does greater $\eta$ affect $A^{*}$?

contexto.p: Here, $A^{world} > 0$ can be thought of as the (constant, for simplicity) world technology frontier. The equation then says that, at every period, the country increases its technology by adopting some new ideas from the world frontier. The rate at which the country can tap into the world frontier depends on its human capital index, $h_{t}$. The rate of adoption also depends on the parameter $\eta > 0$, which captures other factors that might affect research. Finally, in every period, the country "loses" a fraction $\gamma A_{t}$ of its existing technology. This captures that some of the existing ideas might become obsolete over time. The parameter $\gamma > 0$ captures the rate at which ideas "depreciate."

partes.p: [10 points] Suppose the country is initially at a steady state, $k_{0} = k^{*,old}$ and $A_{0} = A^{*,old}$, corresponding to the parameter $h^{old}$. Suppose also that the parameters are such that $A^{*,old} = A^{old}$, so that the initial steady state is exactly the same as that you studied in part b). The only difference is that the technology is now endogenized according to (6). Also as in part b), suppose the country's human capital index suddenly doubles and permanently remains at that higher level, i.e., $h_{t} = 2h^{old}$ for all $t \geq 0$. How much does this change affect the country's output in the long run after it adjusts to the new steady state (in capital as well as in technology)? Is your answer the same as or different than in part b) (for the long-run case)? Provide an intuition.
Consider the neoclassical growth model in continuous time. Output per labor is given by
$$y(t) = k(t)^{\alpha}h(t)^{1-\alpha}$$

where $k(t)$ denotes capital per labor, $h(t)$ denotes human capital per labor, and $\alpha$ denotes the share of capital in output. There is no population growth or technological progress (that is, $n = 0$ and $g = 0)$. Capital per labor thus evolves according to
$$\dot{k}(t) = y(t) - \delta k(t) - c(t)$$

For now, suppose human capital per labor is constant, $h(t) = h^{old}$ for all $t$, for some $h^{old} > 0$. The representative household has per-period utility $u(c) = \frac{c^{1-\theta}-1}{1-\theta}$ for some $\theta > 0$, and her discount rate is $\rho > 0$. The depreciation rate is $\delta$ ∈ (0,1).

partes.p: [5 points] Using a graphical analysis, describe what happens to capital and output, {$k(t)$, y$(t)$}, as the economy transitions to the new steady state.
[5 points] Can you unambiguously tell what happens to consumption in the short-run, $c$(0)? Why or why not? Your answer should describe the economic forces at play.

[10 points] Now consider the more realistic scenario in which, after the new government comes into power, $h(t)$ continuously increases from $h^{old}$ to $h^{new}$ over the time interval [0, t$^{*}]$. A macroeconomist analyzes the effects of the reform. Since she has taken 14.05, she decides to run a growth accounting exercise. Specifically, she considers the following accounting decomposition of the country' growth rate:
$$\frac{\dot{y}(t)}{y(t)} = \alpha \frac{\dot{k}(t)}{k(t)} +(1 - \alpha ) \frac{\dot{h}(t)}{h(t)} + x(t)$$

She calculates the growth rates in this equation, as well as the Solow residual, for each year over the period [0, t$^{*}]$. She then takes averages over the entire period, and obtains the following results for the average growth rate and its decomposition:
• Average $g_{y}$: 2% • Contribution from $k$: 0.66% • Contribution from $h$: 1.33% • Solow residual: 0%

Based on these results, she infers that both physical capital and human capital are im portant drivers of growth over this episode. In her analysis of the country's growth experience she thus decides to focus on savings policies (that might have increased the accumulation of physical capital) as well as education policies (that might have increased the accumulation of human capital). Is her interpretation of the data correct?
